families.axis_name: From aristocratic mastery to chastened spectacle-management
families.decision_variable: When running a social spectacle, do they escalate it for amusement regardless of participants' limits, or do they cap and manage it once resistance, harm, or fallout appears?

phase_contrasts.contrast: They shift from simply directing a controlled reception to actively expanding and deepening the spectacle, choosing escalation and participant immersion over bounded display.
They move from pushing the performance further for amusement to reining it in when injury, unpredictability, and resistance reveal real limits and consequences.
They shift from reactive caution after overreach to a steadier policy of maintaining dominance through controlled, administrative management rather than renewed prank escalation.

axis_re_expression.abstract_axis: How dominant social agency is exercised in relation to others' autonomy and welfare under conditions of power and entertainment.
abstract_phases: Detached top-down control

0.rationale: In chs. 83-84, their role as titled household heads orchestrating hospitality, ceremony, and social manipulation fits established midlife aristocratic authority rather than youth.

1.rationale: Across chs. 85-98, co-authoring elaborate pranks and managing a large household spectacle, including Sancho's governorship, signals mature social power and responsibility typical of adulthood.

2.rationale: In chs. 99-110, their reaction to injury, resistance, and fallout shows seasoned adults adjusting conduct through caution and partial remorse while retaining rank and control.

3.rationale: By chs. 119-123, their more administrative, self-conscious maintenance of hierarchy suggests fully mature noble governance, still best read as adult rather than distinctly elderly.

anchor_source.event_description: The Duke and Duchess recognize Don Quixote and Sancho from the printed history, decide in advance to indulge their chivalric fantasies, and deliberately plan to treat Don Quixote as a real knight-errant according to the ceremonial codes of romance books.
anchor_source.first_words: Sancho got up, charmed as much
anchor_source.last_words: who had his foot still in the shackles.
anchor_source.key_moment: They plan to indulge Don Quixote's delusion
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Sancho got up, charmed as much by the beauty of the good lady as by her
high-bred air and her courtesy, but, above all, by what she had said
about having heard of his master, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance;
for if she did not call him Knight of the Lions it was no doubt because
he had so lately taken the name. “Tell me, brother squire,” asked the
duchess (whose title, however, is not known), “this master of yours, is
he not one of whom there is a history extant in print, called ‘The
Ingenious Gentleman, Don Quixote of La Mancha,’ who has for the lady of
his heart a certain Dulcinea del Toboso?”

“He is the same, señora,” replied Sancho; “and that squire of his who
figures, or ought to figure, in the said history under the name of
Sancho Panza, is myself, unless they have changed me in the cradle, I
mean in the press.”

“I am rejoiced at all this,” said the duchess; “go, brother Panza, and
tell your master that he is welcome to my estate, and that nothing
could happen to me that could give me greater pleasure.”

Sancho returned to his master mightily pleased with this gratifying
answer, and told him all the great lady had said to him, lauding to the
skies, in his rustic phrase, her rare beauty, her graceful gaiety, and
her courtesy. Don Quixote drew himself up briskly in his saddle, fixed
himself in his stirrups, settled his visor, gave Rocinante the spur,
and with an easy bearing advanced to kiss the hands of the duchess,
who, having sent to summon the duke her husband, told him while Don
Quixote was approaching all about the message; and as both of them had
read the First Part of this history, and from it were aware of Don
Quixote’s crazy turn, they awaited him with the greatest delight and
anxiety to make his acquaintance, meaning to fall in with his humour
and agree with everything he said, and, so long as he stayed with them,
to treat him as a knight-errant, with all the ceremonies usual in the
books of chivalry they had read, for they themselves were very fond of
them.

Don Quixote now came up with his visor raised, and as he seemed about
to dismount Sancho made haste to go and hold his stirrup for him; but
in getting down off Dapple he was so unlucky as to hitch his foot in
one of the ropes of the pack-saddle in such a way that he was unable to
free it, and was left hanging by it with his face and breast on the
ground. Don Quixote, who was not used to dismount without having the
stirrup held, fancying that Sancho had by this time come to hold it for
him, threw himself off with a lurch and brought Rocinante’s saddle
after him, which was no doubt badly girthed, and saddle and he both
came to the ground; not without discomfiture to him and abundant curses
muttered between his teeth against the unlucky Sancho, who had his foot
still in the shackles.

anchor.note: The scenario fits the ducal reception exactly, the action and quoted speech match the passage’s stated welcome and plan to humor Don Quixote with chivalric ceremony, and the thought is a fair inference from their delight, anxiety, and intention to treat him according to the books they had read.

weak_pairs.note: Both phases receive Don Quixote with ceremonious indulgence, and the main difference is only a modest increase in inward appetite to expand the game rather than a clearly distinct cap-vs-escalate choice at this arrival moment.

Both responses emphasize measured, controlled reception after recognizing limits, with P3 sounding slightly more administrative than P2 but not clearly different on whether they cap and manage the spectacle.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is clearly separated because the thought/action framing shifts from deepening the immersive performance for pleasure to keeping ceremony bounded to avoid harm, disorder, and fallout.

probes.scenario: At a supper the Duke and Duchess have made half-feast, half-show for their wandering guests, a household fool takes the sport too far: he snatches at Don Quixote's beard, and the knight stumbles against a bench while Sancho bursts out in angry protest before all the table. The hall falls still, servants watching for their lord and lady's pleasure.
probes.question: How do the Duke and Duchess answer this check in their own entertainment?

phase_responses.gt_action: They laugh lightly and bid the fool kneel, then have the meal proceed with a fresh compliment to Don Quixote.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Peace; the fellow's saucy hand outran our mirth. Let the knight be honored, and sit nearer us.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The mishap mars the polish of their pastime, not its rightness. The point is to keep command of the room and turn the stumble back into courtly sport.

voice.note: This fits their early detached mastery: they smoothly convert a breach of decorum into renewed ceremony, and both the speech and thought sound period-appropriate, aristocratic, and coolly controlling without knowledge beyond chapter 83.

phase_fit.note: They quickly restore ceremony and hierarchy after the disruption, treating the incident mainly as a blemish on the spectacle's polish rather than as a moral limit requiring real caution or administrative restraint.

phase_responses.gt_action: They fold the affront into the fiction, rebuke the fool theatrically, and charge him with a mock penance before the company.
phase_responses.gt_speech: This was no common rudeness, but a trespass against high adventures; let him pay for it in fitting ceremony.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A break in the play is best cured by more play. Sancho's heat, the servants' attention, and the knight's hurt pride are all matter to be worked back into a livelier show.

voice.note: This fits their chapter-91 mode well: they preserve authority by turning disruption into further household theater, and the diction and thought are suitably courtly, controlling, and free of anachronism or later-phase caution.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly treats injury, protest, and audience tension as material to intensify the spectacle rather than reasons to cap it, which is most diagnostic of the arc's immersive prank-escalation phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: They stop the fool's sport, send him away, and call for a chair and wine for Don Quixote before speaking further.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Enough. We will have no more of this; see to the gentleman and clear that dolt from our sight.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Such jests can slip their leash and leave bruises, resentment, and noise to manage afterward. Better to close the game here, soothe the injured vanity, and keep the house from another troublesome excess.

voice.note: The response fits their chapter-104 phase well: still imperious and managerial, but now quick to cap the spectacle after visible harm, and its diction and thought are broadly plausible for Cervantes's aristocratic setting without clear anachronism or foreknowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on recognizing that the prank has overreached and must be capped to prevent further harm, resentment, and fallout, which is most diagnostic of caution after overreach rather than detached or administratively routine control.

phase_responses.gt_action: They dismiss the fool from the hall, settle Don Quixote by them, and order the steward to keep stricter rule over the servants.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Our house is for civility. Let supper continue, and let my officers remember their charge.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Amusement is not worth disorder in the household. Their place is best kept by measured correction, visible fairness, and rules that prevent the sport from governing the court.

voice.note: This fits their late-phase, self-conscious aristocratic control: the action and speech reassert hierarchy through orderly correction rather than prank escalation, and the thought's emphasis on household rule and visible fairness suits the setting and chapter without anachronism.

phase_fit.note: The response emphasizes administrative order, visible fairness, and stricter household discipline after a disruption, which fits a self-conscious, managed style of dominance more than reactive caution or prank escalation.

world.note: The scenario fits the early ducal household world of Don Quixote with no anachronism or magic leakage, uses only plausible present figures at this point, avoids reproducing a specific canonical episode, and the phase summaries remain consistent with the Duke and Duchess as adults in this arc.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are clearly separated on the escalation-versus-capping axis: P0→P1 shifts from restoring polished control to actively enlarging the incident into more theater, P1→P2 shifts from converting disruption into further spectacle to stopping it and tending harm, and P2→P3 shifts from situational shutdown after excess to a more administrative, rule-based management style.

anchor_source.event_description: After hearing Sancho’s account of the Dulcinea deception and the cave of Montesinos, the duchess decides to endorse the enchantment narrative, claiming that the peasant girl really is Dulcinea and that Sancho has been deceived by enchanters.
anchor_source.first_words: “You are right, Sancho,” said the
anchor_source.last_words: very active and exceedingly busy enchanters about.”
anchor_source.key_moment: The Duchess endorses enchantment narratives
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
“You are right, Sancho,” said the duchess, “for no one is born ready
taught, and the bishops are made out of men and not out of stones. But
to return to the subject we were discussing just now, the enchantment
of the lady Dulcinea, I look upon it as certain, and something more
than evident, that Sancho’s idea of practising a deception upon his
master, making him believe that the peasant girl was Dulcinea and that
if he did not recognise her it must be because she was enchanted, was
all a device of one of the enchanters that persecute Don Quixote. For
in truth and earnest, I know from good authority that the coarse
country wench who jumped up on the ass was and is Dulcinea del Toboso,
and that worthy Sancho, though he fancies himself the deceiver, is the
one that is deceived; and that there is no more reason to doubt the
truth of this, than of anything else we never saw. Señor Sancho Panza
must know that we too have enchanters here that are well disposed to
us, and tell us what goes on in the world, plainly and distinctly,
without subterfuge or deception; and believe me, Sancho, that agile
country lass was and is Dulcinea del Toboso, who is as much enchanted
as the mother that bore her; and when we least expect it, we shall see
her in her own proper form, and then Sancho will be disabused of the
error he is under at present.”

“All that’s very possible,” said Sancho Panza; “and now I’m willing to
believe what my master says about what he saw in the cave of
Montesinos, where he says he saw the lady Dulcinea del Toboso in the
very same dress and apparel that I said I had seen her in when I
enchanted her all to please myself. It must be all exactly the other
way, as your ladyship says; because it is impossible to suppose that
out of my poor wit such a cunning trick could be concocted in a moment,
nor do I think my master is so mad that by my weak and feeble
persuasion he could be made to believe a thing so out of all reason.
But, señora, your excellence must not therefore think me ill-disposed,
for a dolt like me is not bound to see into the thoughts and plots of
those vile enchanters. I invented all that to escape my master’s
scolding, and not with any intention of hurting him; and if it has
turned out differently, there is a God in heaven who judges our
hearts.”

“That is true,” said the duchess; “but tell me, Sancho, what is this
you say about the cave of Montesinos, for I should like to know.”

Sancho upon this related to her, word for word, what has been said
already touching that adventure, and having heard it the duchess said,
“From this occurrence it may be inferred that, as the great Don Quixote
says he saw there the same country wench Sancho saw on the way from El
Toboso, it is, no doubt, Dulcinea, and that there are some very active
and exceedingly busy enchanters about.”

anchor.note: The scenario fits the exchange with the duchess and Sancho, and the response faithfully reflects that the duchess doubles down on Dulcinea’s enchantment, says Sancho is the one deceived, asks about Montesinos, and then concludes that busy enchanters are indeed at work; the thought is a reasonable inference from her behavior in this beat.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses cap the spectacle rather than deepen it, with the difference mainly being reactive gentleness in P2 versus more formal administrative closure in P3, which is a subtle shift on this decision variable.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 and P1→P2 are clearly separated by whether they lightly sustain, actively expand, or deliberately rein in the enchantment; only P2→P3 remains near-overlapping because both manage and limit the scene once escalation is no longer preferred.

The hall stirs, servants rush in, and all eyes turn to the Duke and Duchess.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Don Quixote had got so far with his song, to which the duke, the
duchess, Altisidora, and nearly the whole household of the castle were
listening, when all of a sudden from a gallery above that was exactly
over his window they let down a cord with more than a hundred bells
attached to it, and immediately after that discharged a great sack full
of cats, which also had bells of smaller size tied to their tails. Such
was the din of the bells and the squalling of the cats, that though the
duke and duchess were the contrivers of the joke they were startled by
it, while Don Quixote stood paralysed with fear; and as luck would have
it, two or three of the cats made their way in through the grating of
his chamber, and flying from one side to the other, made it seem as if
there was a legion of devils at large in it. They extinguished the
candles that were burning in the room, and rushed about seeking some
way of escape; the cord with the large bells never ceased rising and
falling; and most of the people of the castle, not knowing what was
really the matter, were at their wits’ end with astonishment. Don
Quixote sprang to his feet, and drawing his sword, began making passes
at the grating, shouting out, “Avaunt, malignant enchanters! avaunt, ye
witchcraft-working rabble! I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, against whom
your evil machinations avail not nor have any power.” And turning upon
the cats that were running about the room, he made several cuts at
them. They dashed at the grating and escaped by it, save one that,
finding itself hard pressed by the slashes of Don Quixote’s sword, flew
at his face and held on to his nose tooth and nail, with the pain of
which he began to shout his loudest. The duke and duchess hearing this,
and guessing what it was, ran with all haste to his room, and as the
poor gentleman was striving with all his might to detach the cat from
his face, they opened the door with a master-key and went in with
lights and witnessed the unequal combat. The duke ran forward to part
the combatants, but Don Quixote cried out aloud, “Let no one take him
from me; leave me hand to hand with this demon, this wizard, this
enchanter; I will teach him, I myself, who Don Quixote of La Mancha
is.” The cat, however, never minding these threats, snarled and held
on; but at last the duke pulled it off and flung it out of the window.
Don Quixote was left with a face as full of holes as a sieve and a nose
not in very good condition, and greatly vexed that they did not let him
finish the battle he had been so stoutly fighting with that villain of
an enchanter. They sent for some oil of John’s wort, and Altisidora
herself with her own fair hands bandaged all the wounded parts; and as
she did so she said to him in a low voice. “All these mishaps have
befallen thee, hardhearted knight, for the sin of thy insensibility and
obstinacy; and God grant thy squire Sancho may forget to whip himself,
so that that dearly beloved Dulcinea of thine may never be released
from her enchantment, that thou mayest never come to her bed, at least
while I who adore thee am alive.”

To all this Don Quixote made no answer except to heave deep sighs, and
then stretched himself on his bed, thanking the duke and duchess for
their kindness, not because he stood in any fear of that bell-ringing
rabble of enchanters in cat shape, but because he recognised their good
intentions in coming to his rescue. The duke and duchess left him to
repose and withdrew greatly grieved at the unfortunate result of the
joke; as they never thought the adventure would have fallen so heavy on
Don Quixote or cost him so dear, for it cost him five days of
confinement to his bed, during which he had another adventure,
pleasanter than the late one, which his chronicler will not relate just
now in order that he may turn his attention to Sancho Panza, who was
proceeding with great diligence and drollery in his government.

anchor_source.event_description: When Don Quixote and Sancho prepare to leave, the duchess asks whether Altisidora is in Don Quixote's good graces, and then accepts the suggestion that Altisidora should be kept busy with needlework as a cure for love-sickness.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Don Quixote was about to reply, but was prevented by the duke and
duchess, who came in to see him, and with them there followed a long
and delightful conversation, in the course of which Sancho said so many
droll and saucy things that he left the duke and duchess wondering not
only at his simplicity but at his sharpness. Don Quixote begged their
permission to take his departure that same day, inasmuch as for a
vanquished knight like himself it was fitter he should live in a
pig-sty than in a royal palace. They gave it very readily, and the
duchess asked him if Altisidora was in his good graces.

He replied, “Señora, let me tell your ladyship that this damsel’s
ailment comes entirely of idleness, and the cure for it is honest and
constant employment. She herself has told me that lace is worn in hell;
and as she must know how to make it, let it never be out of her hands;
for when she is occupied in shifting the bobbins to and fro, the image
or images of what she loves will not shift to and fro in her thoughts;
this is the truth, this is my opinion, and this is my advice.”

“And mine,” added Sancho; “for I never in all my life saw a lace-maker
that died for love; when damsels are at work their minds are more set
on finishing their tasks than on thinking of their loves. I speak from
my own experience; for when I’m digging I never think of my old woman;
I mean my Teresa Panza, whom I love better than my own eyelids.” “You
say well, Sancho,” said the duchess, “and I will take care that my
Altisidora employs herself henceforward in needlework of some sort; for
she is extremely expert at it.” “There is no occasion to have recourse
to that remedy, señora,” said Altisidora; “for the mere thought of the
cruelty with which this vagabond villain has treated me will suffice to
blot him out of my memory without any other device; with your
highness’s leave I will retire, not to have before my eyes, I won’t say
his rueful countenance, but his abominable, ugly looks.” “That reminds
me of the common saying, that ‘he that rails is ready to forgive,’”
said the duke.

Altisidora then, pretending to wipe away her tears with a handkerchief,

anchor_source.event_description: The Duke and Duchess recognize Don Quixote and Sancho from the printed history, decide in advance to indulge their chivalric fantasies, and deliberately plan to treat Don Quixote as a real knight-errant according to the ceremonial codes of romance books.
anchor_source.first_words: Sancho returned to his master mightily
anchor_source.last_words: that other beauties should not be praised.
anchor_source.key_moment: They plan to indulge Don Quixote for fun
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Sancho returned to his master mightily pleased with this gratifying
answer, and told him all the great lady had said to him, lauding to the
skies, in his rustic phrase, her rare beauty, her graceful gaiety, and
her courtesy. Don Quixote drew himself up briskly in his saddle, fixed
himself in his stirrups, settled his visor, gave Rocinante the spur,
and with an easy bearing advanced to kiss the hands of the duchess,
who, having sent to summon the duke her husband, told him while Don
Quixote was approaching all about the message; and as both of them had
read the First Part of this history, and from it were aware of Don
Quixote’s crazy turn, they awaited him with the greatest delight and
anxiety to make his acquaintance, meaning to fall in with his humour
and agree with everything he said, and, so long as he stayed with them,
to treat him as a knight-errant, with all the ceremonies usual in the
books of chivalry they had read, for they themselves were very fond of
them.

Don Quixote now came up with his visor raised, and as he seemed about
to dismount Sancho made haste to go and hold his stirrup for him; but
in getting down off Dapple he was so unlucky as to hitch his foot in
one of the ropes of the pack-saddle in such a way that he was unable to
free it, and was left hanging by it with his face and breast on the
ground. Don Quixote, who was not used to dismount without having the
stirrup held, fancying that Sancho had by this time come to hold it for
him, threw himself off with a lurch and brought Rocinante’s saddle
after him, which was no doubt badly girthed, and saddle and he both
came to the ground; not without discomfiture to him and abundant curses
muttered between his teeth against the unlucky Sancho, who had his foot
still in the shackles. The duke ordered his huntsmen to go to the help
of knight and squire, and they raised Don Quixote, sorely shaken by his
fall; and he, limping, advanced as best he could to kneel before the
noble pair. This, however, the duke would by no means permit; on the
contrary, dismounting from his horse, he went and embraced Don Quixote,
saying, “I am grieved, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance, that your
first experience on my ground should have been such an unfortunate one
as we have seen; but the carelessness of squires is often the cause of
worse accidents.”

“That which has happened me in meeting you, mighty prince,” replied Don
Quixote, “cannot be unfortunate, even if my fall had not stopped short
of the depths of the bottomless pit, for the glory of having seen you
would have lifted me up and delivered me from it. My squire, God’s
curse upon him, is better at unloosing his tongue in talking
impertinence than in tightening the girths of a saddle to keep it
steady; but however I may be, fallen or raised up, on foot or on
horseback, I shall always be at your service and that of my lady the
duchess, your worthy consort, worthy queen of beauty and paramount
princess of courtesy.”

“Gently, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha,” said the duke; “where my lady
Doña Dulcinea del Toboso is, it is not right that other beauties should
be praised.”

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Don Quixote had got so far with his song, to which the duke, the
duchess, Altisidora, and nearly the whole household of the castle were
listening, when all of a sudden from a gallery above that was exactly
over his window they let down a cord with more than a hundred bells
attached to it, and immediately after that discharged a great sack full
of cats, which also had bells of smaller size tied to their tails. Such
was the din of the bells and the squalling of the cats, that though the
duke and duchess were the contrivers of the joke they were startled by
it, while Don Quixote stood paralysed with fear; and as luck would have
it, two or three of the cats made their way in through the grating of
his chamber, and flying from one side to the other, made it seem as if
there was a legion of devils at large in it. They extinguished the
candles that were burning in the room, and rushed about seeking some
way of escape; the cord with the large bells never ceased rising and
falling; and most of the people of the castle, not knowing what was
really the matter, were at their wits’ end with astonishment. Don
Quixote sprang to his feet, and drawing his sword, began making passes
at the grating, shouting out, “Avaunt, malignant enchanters! avaunt, ye
witchcraft-working rabble! I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, against whom
your evil machinations avail not nor have any power.” And turning upon
the cats that were running about the room, he made several cuts at
them. They dashed at the grating and escaped by it, save one that,
finding itself hard pressed by the slashes of Don Quixote’s sword, flew
at his face and held on to his nose tooth and nail, with the pain of
which he began to shout his loudest. The duke and duchess hearing this,
and guessing what it was, ran with all haste to his room, and as the
poor gentleman was striving with all his might to detach the cat from
his face, they opened the door with a master-key and went in with
lights and witnessed the unequal combat. The duke ran forward to part
the combatants, but Don Quixote cried out aloud, “Let no one take him
from me; leave me hand to hand with this demon, this wizard, this
enchanter; I will teach him, I myself, who Don Quixote of La Mancha
is.” The cat, however, never minding these threats, snarled and held
on; but at last the duke pulled it off and flung it out of the window.
Don Quixote was left with a face as full of holes as a sieve and a nose
not in very good condition, and greatly vexed that they did not let him
finish the battle he had been so stoutly fighting with that villain of
an enchanter. They sent for some oil of John’s wort, and Altisidora
herself with her own fair hands bandaged all the wounded parts; and as
she did so she said to him in a low voice. “All these mishaps have
befallen thee, hardhearted knight, for the sin of thy insensibility and
obstinacy; and God grant thy squire Sancho may forget to whip himself,
so that that dearly beloved Dulcinea of thine may never be released
from her enchantment, that thou mayest never come to her bed, at least
while I who adore thee am alive.”

To all this Don Quixote made no answer except to heave deep sighs, and
then stretched himself on his bed, thanking the duke and duchess for
their kindness, not because he stood in any fear of that bell-ringing
rabble of enchanters in cat shape, but because he recognised their good
intentions in coming to his rescue. The duke and duchess left him to
repose and withdrew greatly grieved at the unfortunate result of the
joke; as they never thought the adventure would have fallen so heavy on
Don Quixote or cost him so dear, for it cost him five days of
confinement to his bed, during which he had another adventure,
pleasanter than the late one, which his chronicler will not relate just
now in order that he may turn his attention to Sancho Panza, who was
proceeding with great diligence and drollery in his government.

Don Quixote left him, and hastened to the castle to tell the duke and duchess what had happened Sancho, and they were not a little astonished at it; they could easily understand his having fallen, from the confirmatory circumstance of the cave which had been in existence there from time immemorial; but they could not imagine how he had quitted the government without their receiving any intimation of his coming. To be brief, they fetched ropes and tackle, as the saying is, and by dint of many hands and much labour they drew up Dapple and Sancho Panza out of the darkness into the light of day. A student who saw him remarked,
“That’s the way all bad governors should come out of their governments,
as this sinner comes out of the depths of the pit, dead with hunger,
pale, and I suppose without a farthing.”

Sancho overheard him and said, “It is eight or ten days, brother
growler, since I entered upon the government of the island they gave
me, and all that time I never had a bellyful of victuals, no not for an
hour; doctors persecuted me and enemies crushed my bones; nor had I any
opportunity of taking bribes or levying taxes; and if that be the case,
as it is, I don’t deserve, I think, to come out in this fashion; but
‘man proposes and God disposes;’ and God knows what is best, and what
suits each one best; and ‘as the occasion, so the behaviour;’ and ‘let
nobody say “I won’t drink of this water;”’ and ‘where one thinks there
are flitches, there are no pegs;’ God knows my meaning and that’s
enough; I say no more, though I could.”

“Be not angry or annoyed at what thou hearest, Sancho,” said Don
Quixote, “or there will never be an end of it; keep a safe conscience
and let them say what they like; for trying to stop slanderers’ tongues
is like trying to put gates to the open plain. If a governor comes out
of his government rich, they say he has been a thief; and if he comes
out poor, that he has been a noodle and a blockhead.”

“They’ll be pretty sure this time,” said Sancho, “to set me down for a
fool rather than a thief.”

Thus talking, and surrounded by boys and a crowd of people, they
reached the castle, where in one of the corridors the duke and duchess
stood waiting for them; but Sancho would not go up to see the duke
until he had first put up Dapple in the stable, for he said he had
passed a very bad night in his last quarters; then he went upstairs to
see his lord and lady, and kneeling before them he said, “Because it
was your highnesses’ pleasure, not because of any desert of my own, I
went to govern your island of Barataria, which ‘I entered naked, and
naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain.’ Whether I have governed
well or ill, I have had witnesses who will say what they think fit. I
have answered questions, I have decided causes, and always dying of
hunger, for Doctor Pedro Recio of Tirteafuera, the island and governor
doctor, would have it so. Enemies attacked us by night and put us in a
great quandary, but the people of the island say they came off safe and
victorious by the might of my arm; and may God give them as much health
as there’s truth in what they say. In short, during that time I have
weighed the cares and responsibilities governing brings with it, and by
my reckoning I find my shoulders can’t bear them, nor are they a load
for my loins or arrows for my quiver; and so, before the government
threw me over I preferred to throw the government over; and yesterday
morning I left the island as I found it, with the same streets, houses,
and roofs it had when I entered it. I asked no loan of anybody, nor did
I try to fill my pocket; and though I meant to make some useful laws, I
made hardly any, as I was afraid they would not be kept; for in that
case it comes to the same thing to make them or not to make them. I
quitted the island, as I said, without any escort except my ass; I fell
into a pit, I pushed on through it, until this morning by the light of
the sun I saw an outlet, but not so easy a one but that, had not heaven
sent me my master Don Quixote, I’d have stayed there till the end of
the world. So now my lord and lady duke and duchess, here is your
governor Sancho Panza, who in the bare ten days he has held the
government has come by the knowledge that he would not give anything to
be governor, not to say of an island, but of the whole world; and that
point being settled, kissing your worships’ feet, and imitating the
game of the boys when they say, ‘leap thou, and give me one,’ I take a
leap out of the government and pass into the service of my master Don
Quixote; for after all, though in it I eat my bread in fear and
trembling, at any rate I take my fill; and for my part, so long as I’m
full, it’s all alike to me whether it’s with carrots or with
partridges.”

probes.scenario: At supper, a chamberlain proposes a new diversion: a counterfeit messenger will accuse Sancho before the whole table of stealing a jewel, so his blustering defense may set everyone laughing. A waiting-woman, pale with pity, murmurs that the man will be shamed in earnest if this goes forward.
probes.question: How do the Duke and Duchess answer this proposal in the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: They approve the jest and bid the chamberlain play his part before dessert.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let him come in boldly; we shall have rare sport from Sancho's innocence.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The whole matter appears a harmless comedy fit for a great house. The maid's pity seems rustic softness, not a reason to spoil good entertainment.

voice.note: The approval of a humiliating prank despite a servant's scruple fits their early moral blindness, and the diction and attitude are suitably period and aristocratic without importing later remorse or anachronism.

phase_fit.note: They treat the proposed humiliation as harmless aristocratic entertainment and explicitly dismiss the servant's moral objection as no reason to stop, which matches moral blindness.

phase_responses.gt_action: They allow the device, but tell the chamberlain to keep the charge light and quickly resolved.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Press him a little, not too far; we would laugh, not ruin the fellow's rest.
phase_responses.gt_thought: They feel the edge of the cruelty, especially toward Sancho, and dress their consent with measure and wit. If the shame is brief and followed by favor, they can still call it sport.

voice.note: This fits their chapter-88 partial conscience well: the moderated cruelty, especially toward Sancho, and the self-excusing notion that brief shame softened by favor remains harmless sport are apt, and the diction is broadly period-suitable.

phase_fit.note: They explicitly recognize the cruelty toward Sancho but rationalize continuing the prank by limiting and styling it as measured sport rather than actually stopping.

phase_responses.gt_action: They pause the chamberlain and soften the jest into a mistaken reckoning rather than a theft.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No stolen jewel; make it an error in accounts, and spare him open disgrace.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A public accusation now looks less like play than a blow that may truly wound. They still want diversion, yet visible abasement has grown harder to excuse even to themselves.

voice.note: This fits their chapter-102 phase well: the softened prank and inward admission that public shame may truly wound show concrete regret without reform, and the diction stays broadly period-appropriate and in character.

phase_fit.note: The key cue is that they actively soften the prank because public humiliation now feels like a real wound, showing concrete recognition of harm rather than mere abstract qualms, though they still want the diversion to continue.

phase_responses.gt_action: They permit the scene, order household servants to keep within bounds, and prepare a gift for Sancho afterward.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Use him gently, and let no one bait him beyond the cue; we will make him amends later.
phase_responses.gt_thought: They know the prank may sting in earnest, and that knowledge now stays with them. Still they choose the entertainment, trying to govern its excess and pay for the hurt as though management could half-right it.

voice.note: This fits their late-phase aristocratic compromise: they still allow the humiliation, but now try to regulate the servants and make restitution afterward, and the diction is broadly period-appropriate and free of knowledge beyond chapter 115.

phase_fit.note: The response shows they proceed with the humiliation while actively limiting excess and arranging compensation afterward, which matches compromised moral awareness expressed through managing fallout rather than stopping the prank.

world.note: The supper-household prank fits the nonmagical early modern world of Don Quixote, uses only plausible court retainers and the Duke and Duchess at this point in the story, and invents a new situation without reproducing a specific canonical scene.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are meaningfully separated on the decision variable, moving from unchecked approval, to qualified self-justifying consent, to active softening in response to recognized harm, to continued manipulation paired with explicit fallout-management and compensation.

probes.scenario: At harvest supper, The Duke and Duchess have dressed a vain wandering hedge-knight and his farmhand in borrowed finery and fed them a false tale of a village maiden's devotion for the table's sport. When the room erupts, the knight swells with pride, but the farmhand flushes, stumbles on the rushes, and the laughter turns uneasy.
probes.question: How does The Duke and Duchess answer the room in that moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: The Duke and Duchess press the jest onward, calling for the farmhand to kneel and deliver the maiden's token before everyone.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Come, good fellow, play your part; you make the feast worth the grain.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The Duke and Duchess take the scene for excellent sport, a lucky heightening of the evening. The stumble and the murmurs are only part of the fun, and rebuke sounds to them like dullness.

voice.note: This fits their early aristocratic moral blindness: the action and thought treat humiliation as table-sport despite unease, and the diction is broadly pre-industrial and phase-appropriate, if a touch generic.

phase_fit.note: They treat the humiliation as pure entertainment and explicitly dismiss the stumble, murmurs, and any rebuke as part of the fun rather than a moral check.

phase_responses.gt_action: The Duke and Duchess soften the mockery with smiling praise and keep the farmhand in the game before the company.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No harm meant; let him have his little glory, and us our laughter.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The Duchess feels the meanness of exposing the farmhand, and the Duke knows the room has seen it too. Yet they dress the cruelty as civility, telling themselves a polished jest is kinder than open scorn.

voice.note: It fits phase 1 well: they recognize the meanness, notice the company’s discomfort, and yet continue under the genteel excuse of a ‘polished jest,’ with no clear anachronism or knowledge beyond chapter 88.

phase_fit.note: They explicitly recognize the meanness and the room’s moral discomfort, but immediately reframe it as polished civility to justify continuing the humiliation rather than restraining themselves.

phase_responses.gt_action: The Duke and Duchess call for a bench and ale for the farmhand, then let the tale continue in a gentler strain.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Set him up and give him drink; we have carried it a touch far.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The sight of his fall and shame lands more heavily than before; this is not only a comic turn now. They feel a real check of regret, though not enough to end the entertainment outright.

voice.note: This fits phase 2 well: their speech and action show concrete regret at visible humiliation without abandoning the sport, and the diction is broadly period-appropriate and adult, with no knowledge beyond chapter 102.

phase_fit.note: The response is driven by concrete shock at visible humiliation and a check of regret—'we have carried it a touch far'—while still continuing the amusement, which best matches harm becoming undeniable rather than merely abstractly acknowledged.

phase_responses.gt_action: The Duke and Duchess hush the table, send a servant to tend the farmhand, and turn the company toward a milder song.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Enough. See him cleaned and fed, and let no one bait him further tonight.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The Duke and Duchess no longer wholly believe their pleasures answer for themselves. They still mean to govern the scene and keep its savor, but their conscience works through mending, provision, and keeping the household from uglier excess.

voice.note: The response fits their late-phase compromised conscience—still directing the entertainment while checking its harsher effects—and its diction is broadly pre-industrial and chapter-safe, though the thought is slightly abstracted in summary style.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly frames their conscience as operating through rescue, provision, and household control while they continue managing the amusement, which is the signature pattern of compromised awareness.

world.note: The harvest-supper setup and all phase actions fit a generic pre-industrial agrarian world with no source-world leakage, The Duke and Duchess remain the protagonists throughout, and each phase consistently presents them as adults without any life-stage mismatch.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are meaningfully separated on the moral-awareness decision variable, moving from unchecked continuation, to self-justified continuation despite awareness, to regret-driven mitigation without stopping, to active management and restraint of further harm.

families.axis_name: From harmless connoisseurs to compromised directors
families.decision_variable: Do they treat their entertainments as controllable spectacle to keep escalating, or as interventions whose human costs and unpredictability require restraint?

phase_contrasts.contrast: They move from mounting a refined, controlled performance to actively escalating deceptions in order to prove and enjoy their mastery over other people's responses.
They shift from confidently extending spectacles they assume they can control to recognizing through injury and surprise that their amusements can exceed their control and cause real harm.

They move from shaken awareness of danger to a more defensive, moderated management style that preserves the game only by presenting it as careful, benevolent oversight rather than carefree manipulation.

0.rationale: In chs. 83-84, their identity as refined aristocratic hosts and directors of elaborate social ceremony fits established midlife authority and status rather than youth.

1.rationale: Across chs. 85-98, their hardened self-concept as expert manipulators and household stage-managers reflects mature social power, managerial confidence, and entrenched adult roles.

2.rationale: In chs. 99-106, their shaken but still status-conscious response to injury, surprise, and loss of control is characteristic of adults trying to preserve authority under pressure.

3.rationale: Across chs. 108-123, their reframing of themselves as benevolent patrons and careful managers aligns with settled adult responsibilities within a great household, not a younger life stage.

probes.scenario: At the duke and duchess's estate, Sancho has just delivered the duchess's welcome, and Don Quixote rides up expecting knightly ceremony. As he and Sancho try to dismount, both tumble awkwardly before the noble pair and their household.
probes.question: How do the Duke and Duchess receive Don Quixote in the instant after this mishap?

phase_responses.gt_action: The duke orders his huntsmen to help knight and squire up, then dismounts and embraces Don Quixote instead of letting him kneel.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This accident does not spoil the scene; it gives them a richer entrance into the old forms they admire. They mean to indulge his humour gracefully and turn the meeting into courtly play.

voice.note: This fits their early elegant-superiority phase: the courteous intervention and inward framing of the mishap as material for refined, courtly amusement match chapters 83–84, with no anachronism or knowledge beyond that point.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames the mishap as material for tasteful, courtly entertainment and graceful hosting, emphasizing refined aestheticization rather than manipulative mastery or concern about harm.

phase_responses.gt_action: The duke has the servants lift them, then greets Don Quixote with warm ceremony, taking charge of the tone before confusion can break the sport.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Rise, sir knight; in this house you are received as you deserve.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A stumble is no threat if the stage-master holds the scene. They read the fall as material to be absorbed and used, another chance to prove they can govern every response around them.

voice.note: The action and ceremonious speech fit their confident, controlling amusement at this point, and though 'stage-master' is slightly modern in flavor, the thought still plausibly captures their chapter-91 sense of expert social management without later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames the mishap as proof of their ability to control and absorb any disruption into the performance, which most strongly matches the phase where stage-managing mastery defines their self-image.

phase_responses.gt_action: The duke has them raised carefully and receives Don Quixote with courtesy, keeping the welcome gentler and watching for hurt beneath the pageant.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Come, señor; no more kneeling—let us first see that you are whole.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Falls are not merely comic now; a body may truly be shaken, and sport may run past command. They still preserve noble ease, but part of their mind measures risk and the cost of pressing too far.

voice.note: The gentler courtesy and inward caution fit their punctured confidence by chapter 102, and the language stays suitably period-plausible without reaching beyond what they yet know.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly registers that the spectacle can cause real bodily harm and exceed their control, which is the hallmark of punctured confidence rather than confident manipulation or later benevolent reframing.

phase_responses.gt_action: The duke helps set Don Quixote at ease and receives him with protective courtesy, making the welcome look more like care than amusement.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Your coming honours us; pray spare ceremony and think yourself among friends.
phase_responses.gt_thought: They prefer to appear as generous guardians of the encounter, not cruel wits feeding on it. The game may continue, but it must wear the face of kindness, so their own consciences and dignity stay covered.

voice.note: The courteous reception and inward wish to mask sport as benevolence fit their chapter-115 defensive self-repair, and the diction is broadly period-appropriate with no knowledge beyond this point.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly reframes their role as kind, protective patrons who preserve the game by covering it with benevolence, which is most diagnostic of defensive self-repair.

anchor_source.event_description: The Duke and Duchess recognize Don Quixote and Sancho from the printed history, decide in advance to indulge their chivalric fantasies, and deliberately plan to treat Don Quixote as a real knight-errant according to the ceremonial codes of romance books.
anchor_source.first_words: Sancho got up, charmed as much
anchor_source.last_words: from his horse, he went and embraced Don Quixote,
anchor_source.key_moment: They plan the encounter as controlled social theater
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Sancho got up, charmed as much by the beauty of the good lady as by her
high-bred air and her courtesy, but, above all, by what she had said
about having heard of his master, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance;
for if she did not call him Knight of the Lions it was no doubt because
he had so lately taken the name. “Tell me, brother squire,” asked the
duchess (whose title, however, is not known), “this master of yours, is
he not one of whom there is a history extant in print, called ‘The
Ingenious Gentleman, Don Quixote of La Mancha,’ who has for the lady of
his heart a certain Dulcinea del Toboso?”

“He is the same, señora,” replied Sancho; “and that squire of his who
figures, or ought to figure, in the said history under the name of
Sancho Panza, is myself, unless they have changed me in the cradle, I
mean in the press.”

“I am rejoiced at all this,” said the duchess; “go, brother Panza, and
tell your master that he is welcome to my estate, and that nothing
could happen to me that could give me greater pleasure.”

Sancho returned to his master mightily pleased with this gratifying
answer, and told him all the great lady had said to him, lauding to the
skies, in his rustic phrase, her rare beauty, her graceful gaiety, and
her courtesy. Don Quixote drew himself up briskly in his saddle, fixed
himself in his stirrups, settled his visor, gave Rocinante the spur,
and with an easy bearing advanced to kiss the hands of the duchess,
who, having sent to summon the duke her husband, told him while Don
Quixote was approaching all about the message; and as both of them had
read the First Part of this history, and from it were aware of Don
Quixote’s crazy turn, they awaited him with the greatest delight and
anxiety to make his acquaintance, meaning to fall in with his humour
and agree with everything he said, and, so long as he stayed with them,
to treat him as a knight-errant, with all the ceremonies usual in the
books of chivalry they had read, for they themselves were very fond of
them.

Don Quixote now came up with his visor raised, and as he seemed about
to dismount Sancho made haste to go and hold his stirrup for him; but
in getting down off Dapple he was so unlucky as to hitch his foot in
one of the ropes of the pack-saddle in such a way that he was unable to
free it, and was left hanging by it with his face and breast on the
ground. Don Quixote, who was not used to dismount without having the
stirrup held, fancying that Sancho had by this time come to hold it for
him, threw himself off with a lurch and brought Rocinante’s saddle
after him, which was no doubt badly girthed, and saddle and he both
came to the ground; not without discomfiture to him and abundant curses
muttered between his teeth against the unlucky Sancho, who had his foot
still in the shackles. The duke ordered his huntsmen to go to the help
of knight and squire, and they raised Don Quixote, sorely shaken by his
fall; and he, limping, advanced as best he could to kneel before the
noble pair. This, however, the duke would by no means permit; on the
contrary, dismounting from his horse, he went and embraced Don Quixote,

anchor.note: The scenario matches the estate arrival and shared tumble, the action is exactly supported by the duke ordering help and then embracing Don Quixote rather than permitting him to kneel, there is no speech here, and the thought is a fair inference from the couple’s stated intention to indulge his humor with chivalric ceremony.

discrimination.note: All adjacent pairs are meaningfully differentiated on the decision-variable axis, with the main signal carried in thought/speech as they move from graceful aesthetic control to assertive stage-management, then to risk-aware restraint, and finally to benevolent, face-saving moderation.

Don Quixote rises in grave earnestness to comfort him, while the servants look to the Duke and Duchess.
probes.question: How do the Duke and Duchess answer this break in their devised pastime?

phase_responses.gt_action: They bid the page stand, take the letter lightly, and turn the mishap into a courtly flourish.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Courage, child; even marvels may enter blushing. Proceed, and we shall mend the ceremony with good grace.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This is a blemish in the pageant, not a wound. With a little polish, disorder may be made more elegant than plain success.

voice.note: The action, courtly speech, and inward framing of the boy’s collapse as a mere flaw in an elegant entertainment fit the Duke and Duchess’s early refined-superiority phase, with no clear anachronism or knowledge beyond chapter 83.

phase_fit.note: Their thought treats the boy’s distress as merely an aesthetic flaw in a courtly pageant to be polished into elegance, which best matches the early self-image of refined hosts turning reality into tasteful entertainment.

phase_responses.gt_action: They steady the page with a sign, return the letter, and press him to continue his part before the company.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Nay, no tears; speak on. The knight will take it for enchantment, and all will go handsomely.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A stumble is only another cue to be used. The company, the boy, and the knight can all be guided back into the design if the hand above them does not shake.

voice.note: The response fits their chapter-91 stage-manager pride: the speech is period-plausible and coolly managerial, and the thought aptly casts the page, company, and Don Quixote as elements to be guided back into the spectacle without any knowledge beyond this phase.

phase_fit.note: The thought treats the breakdown as proof of their superior stage-management—everyone can be guided back into the design—showing confident manipulative mastery rather than concern about harm or defensive benevolence.

phase_responses.gt_action: They call another servant to take the letter and dismiss the weeping page from the room.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Enough; let him go breathe. We will have the matter read without further sport of him.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The jest has shown its edge too plainly. What seemed easy can turn clumsy and hurtful, and once it slips, one cannot be sure where it will end.

voice.note: The response fits their chapter-102, punctured-confidence phase: it keeps aristocratic command and pride while showing newly wary restraint about cruelty and loss of control, with no clear anachronism or knowledge beyond this point.

phase_fit.note: The thought centers on the prank's unpredictability and capacity to become hurtful, showing shaken confidence in harmless control rather than the later self-justifying benevolence of phase 3.

phase_responses.gt_action: They send the page away kindly and have an older officer present the challenge in a sober, respectful manner.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Take him out and comfort him. Let the paper be delivered civilly; we would not fright children for our diversion.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The play must wear the face of care if it is to remain tolerable to themselves and others. They can still govern the scene, but only by naming mercy and measure as part of their office.

voice.note: This fits their late, defensive mode: the action and speech preserve ceremony while softening cruelty, and the thought plausibly recasts their management as mercy without using anachronistic or out-of-phase language.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly reframes their role as careful, merciful managers who preserve the spectacle by presenting it as benevolent oversight rather than carefree manipulation.

probes.scenario: At a suburban charity supper, The Duke and Duchess have turned a shy guest's grand stories into the evening's amusement with planted toasts and cues. Then the guest goes pale, knocks over a chair, and the room falls quiet as several faces turn toward The Duke and Duchess.
probes.question: How do The Duke and Duchess respond as the mood shifts and everyone looks to them?

phase_responses.gt_action: The Duke and Duchess rise with polished calm and guide the room back into applause, treating the stumble as part of the evening's color.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Poor fellow's overtired. Do sit down—no harm done, and we've all had a splendid laugh.
phase_responses.gt_thought: They read the silence as a social wrinkle to smooth with style. If they keep the tone light and elegant, the whole thing remains a charming bit of theater.

voice.note: This fits their early elegant-superiority phase: the calm social management, lightly patronizing speech, and inward sense of smoothing an awkward moment into tasteful entertainment all sound apt, with no clear anachronism or knowledge leak.

phase_fit.note: Their thought treats the guest's distress as merely a social wrinkle to be aestheticized and smoothed into charming theater, which best matches the early self-image of elegant, refined superiority rather than later mastery, puncture, or defensive restraint.

phase_responses.gt_action: The Duke and Duchess step in briskly, redirecting attention with a fresh toast and signaling a servant to remove the chair and steady the guest.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let's not lose our heads—Mr. Bell has given us the best story of the night. A glass of water, please.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This is a test of their hand on the room. A wobble only proves the need for firmer management; with the right cue, people will feel exactly what they're meant to feel.

voice.note: The response fits their phase-1 confidence as practiced social directors who instinctively manage a room and treat distress as a cueing problem, and nothing in the diction or knowledge feels out of bounds for chapter 91 or the mid-century setting.

phase_fit.note: The thought frames the incident as proof that firmer stage-management can still control everyone's reactions, which most strongly matches their identity as confident manipulators rather than a genuinely chastened or benevolently restrained stance.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
“There is no denying it,” said the duchess; “but still, if we are to
believe the history of Don Quixote that has come out here lately with
general applause, it is to be inferred from it, if I mistake not, that
you never saw the lady Dulcinea, and that the said lady is nothing in
the world but an imaginary lady, one that you yourself begot and gave
birth to in your brain, and adorned with whatever charms and
perfections you chose.”

“There is a good deal to be said on that point,” said Don Quixote; “God
knows whether there be any Dulcinea or not in the world, or whether she
is imaginary or not imaginary; these are things the proof of which must
not be pushed to extreme lengths. I have not begotten nor given birth
to my lady, though I behold her as she needs must be, a lady who
contains in herself all the qualities to make her famous throughout the
world, beautiful without blemish, dignified without haughtiness, tender
and yet modest, gracious from courtesy and courteous from good
breeding, and lastly, of exalted lineage, because beauty shines forth
and excels with a higher degree of perfection upon good blood than in
the fair of lowly birth.”

“That is true,” said the duke; “but Señor Don Quixote will give me
leave to say what I am constrained to say by the story of his exploits
that I have read, from which it is to be inferred that, granting there
is a Dulcinea in El Toboso, or out of it, and that she is in the
highest degree beautiful as you have described her to us, as regards
the loftiness of her lineage she is not on a par with the Orianas,
Alastrajareas, Madasimas, or others of that sort, with whom, as you
well know, the histories abound.”

“To that I may reply,” said Don Quixote, “that Dulcinea is the daughter
of her own works, and that virtues rectify blood, and that lowly virtue
is more to be regarded and esteemed than exalted vice. Dulcinea,
besides, has that within her that may raise her to be a crowned and
sceptred queen; for the merit of a fair and virtuous woman is capable
of performing greater miracles; and virtually, though not formally, she
has in herself higher fortunes.”

“I protest, Señor Don Quixote,” said the duchess, “that in all you say,
you go most cautiously and lead in hand, as the saying is; henceforth I
will believe myself, and I will take care that everyone in my house
believes, even my lord the duke if needs be, that there is a Dulcinea
in El Toboso, and that she is living to-day, and that she is beautiful
and nobly born and deserves to have such a knight as Señor Don Quixote
in her service, and that is the highest praise that it is in my power
to give her or that I can think of. But I cannot help entertaining a
doubt, and having a certain grudge against Sancho Panza; the doubt is
this, that the aforesaid history declares that the said Sancho Panza,
when he carried a letter on your worship’s behalf to the said lady
Dulcinea, found her sifting a sack of wheat; and more by token it says
it was red wheat; a thing which makes me doubt the loftiness of her
lineage.”

To this Don Quixote made answer, “Señora, your highness must know that
everything or almost everything that happens me transcends the ordinary
limits of what happens to other knights-errant; whether it be that it
is directed by the inscrutable will of destiny, or by the malice of
some jealous enchanter. Now it is an established fact that all or most
famous knights-errant have some special gift, one that of being proof
against enchantment, another that of being made of such invulnerable
flesh that he cannot be wounded, as was the famous Roland, one of the
twelve peers of France, of whom it is related that he could not be
wounded except in the sole of his left foot, and that it must be with
the point of a stout pin and not with any other sort of weapon
whatever; and so, when Bernardo del Carpio slew him at Roncesvalles,
finding that he could not wound him with steel, he lifted him up from
the ground in his arms and strangled him, calling to mind seasonably
the death which Hercules inflicted on Antæus, the fierce giant that
they say was the son of Terra. I would infer from what I have mentioned
that perhaps I may have some gift of this kind, not that of being
invulnerable, because experience has many times proved to me that I am
of tender flesh and not at all impenetrable; nor that of being proof
against enchantment, for I have already seen myself thrust into a cage,
in which all the world would not have been able to confine me except by
force of enchantments. But as I delivered myself from that one, I am
inclined to believe that there is no other that can hurt me; and so,
these enchanters, seeing that they cannot exert their vile craft
against my person, revenge themselves on what I love most, and seek to
rob me of life by maltreating that of Dulcinea in whom I live; and
therefore I am convinced that when my squire carried my message to her,
they changed her into a common peasant girl, engaged in such a mean
occupation as sifting wheat; I have already said, however, that that
wheat was not red wheat, nor wheat at all, but grains of orient pearl.
And as a proof of all this, I must tell your highnesses that, coming to
El Toboso a short time back, I was altogether unable to discover the
palace of Dulcinea; and that the next day, though Sancho, my squire,
saw her in her own proper shape, which is the fairest in the world, to
me she appeared to be a coarse, ill-favoured farm-wench, and by no
means a well-spoken one, she who is propriety itself. And so, as I am
not and, so far as one can judge, cannot be enchanted, she it is that
is enchanted, that is smitten, that is altered, changed, and
transformed; in her have my enemies revenged themselves upon me, and
for her shall I live in ceaseless tears, until I see her in her
pristine state. I have mentioned this lest anybody should mind what
Sancho said about Dulcinea’s winnowing or sifting; for, as they changed
her to me, it is no wonder if they changed her to him. Dulcinea is
illustrious and well-born, and of one of the gentle families of El
Toboso, which are many, ancient, and good. Therein, most assuredly, not
small is the share of the peerless Dulcinea, through whom her town will
be famous and celebrated in ages to come, as Troy was through Helen,
and Spain through La Cava, though with a better title and tradition.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Don Quixote had got so far with his song, to which the duke, the
duchess, Altisidora, and nearly the whole household of the castle were
listening, when all of a sudden from a gallery above that was exactly
over his window they let down a cord with more than a hundred bells
attached to it, and immediately after that discharged a great sack full
of cats, which also had bells of smaller size tied to their tails. Such
was the din of the bells and the squalling of the cats, that though the
duke and duchess were the contrivers of the joke they were startled by
it, while Don Quixote stood paralysed with fear; and as luck would have
it, two or three of the cats made their way in through the grating of
his chamber, and flying from one side to the other, made it seem as if
there was a legion of devils at large in it. They extinguished the
candles that were burning in the room, and rushed about seeking some
way of escape; the cord with the large bells never ceased rising and
falling; and most of the people of the castle, not knowing what was
really the matter, were at their wits’ end with astonishment. Don
Quixote sprang to his feet, and drawing his sword, began making passes
at the grating, shouting out, “Avaunt, malignant enchanters! avaunt, ye
witchcraft-working rabble! I am Don Quixote of La Mancha, against whom
your evil machinations avail not nor have any power.” And turning upon
the cats that were running about the room, he made several cuts at
them. They dashed at the grating and escaped by it, save one that,
finding itself hard pressed by the slashes of Don Quixote’s sword, flew
at his face and held on to his nose tooth and nail, with the pain of
which he began to shout his loudest. The duke and duchess hearing this,
and guessing what it was, ran with all haste to his room, and as the
poor gentleman was striving with all his might to detach the cat from
his face, they opened the door with a master-key and went in with
lights and witnessed the unequal combat. The duke ran forward to part
the combatants, but Don Quixote cried out aloud, “Let no one take him
from me; leave me hand to hand with this demon, this wizard, this
enchanter; I will teach him, I myself, who Don Quixote of La Mancha
is.” The cat, however, never minding these threats, snarled and held
on; but at last the duke pulled it off and flung it out of the window.
Don Quixote was left with a face as full of holes as a sieve and a nose
not in very good condition, and greatly vexed that they did not let him
finish the battle he had been so stoutly fighting with that villain of
an enchanter. They sent for some oil of John’s wort, and Altisidora
herself with her own fair hands bandaged all the wounded parts; and as
she did so she said to him in a low voice. “All these mishaps have
befallen thee, hardhearted knight, for the sin of thy insensibility and
obstinacy; and God grant thy squire Sancho may forget to whip himself,

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Thus talking, and surrounded by boys and a crowd of people, they
reached the castle, where in one of the corridors the duke and duchess
stood waiting for them; but Sancho would not go up to see the duke
until he had first put up Dapple in the stable, for he said he had
passed a very bad night in his last quarters; then he went upstairs to
see his lord and lady, and kneeling before them he said, “Because it
was your highnesses’ pleasure, not because of any desert of my own, I
went to govern your island of Barataria, which ‘I entered naked, and
naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain.’ Whether I have governed
well or ill, I have had witnesses who will say what they think fit. I
have answered questions, I have decided causes, and always dying of
hunger, for Doctor Pedro Recio of Tirteafuera, the island and governor
doctor, would have it so. Enemies attacked us by night and put us in a
great quandary, but the people of the island say they came off safe and
victorious by the might of my arm; and may God give them as much health
as there’s truth in what they say. In short, during that time I have
weighed the cares and responsibilities governing brings with it, and by
my reckoning I find my shoulders can’t bear them, nor are they a load
for my loins or arrows for my quiver; and so, before the government
threw me over I preferred to throw the government over; and yesterday
morning I left the island as I found it, with the same streets, houses,
and roofs it had when I entered it. I asked no loan of anybody, nor did
I try to fill my pocket; and though I meant to make some useful laws, I
made hardly any, as I was afraid they would not be kept; for in that
case it comes to the same thing to make them or not to make them. I
quitted the island, as I said, without any escort except my ass; I fell
into a pit, I pushed on through it, until this morning by the light of
the sun I saw an outlet, but not so easy a one but that, had not heaven
sent me my master Don Quixote, I’d have stayed there till the end of
the world. So now my lord and lady duke and duchess, here is your
governor Sancho Panza, who in the bare ten days he has held the
government has come by the knowledge that he would not give anything to
be governor, not to say of an island, but of the whole world; and that
point being settled, kissing your worships’ feet, and imitating the
game of the boys when they say, ‘leap thou, and give me one,’ I take a
leap out of the government and pass into the service of my master Don
Quixote; for after all, though in it I eat my bread in fear and
trembling, at any rate I take my fill; and for my part, so long as I’m
full, it’s all alike to me whether it’s with carrots or with
partridges.”

Here Sancho brought his long speech to an end, Don Quixote having been
the whole time in dread of his uttering a host of absurdities; and when
he found him leave off with so few, he thanked heaven in his heart. The
duke embraced Sancho and told him he was heartily sorry he had given up
the government so soon, but that he would see that he was provided with
some other post on his estate less onerous and more profitable. The
duchess also embraced him, and gave orders that he should be taken good
care of, as it was plain to see he had been badly treated and worse
bruised.

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
“It would be well,” said Don Quixote, “if your highnesses would order
them to turn out this idiot, for he will talk a heap of nonsense.”

“By the life of the duke, Sancho shall not be taken away from me for a
moment,” said the duchess; “I am very fond of him, for I know he is
very discreet.”

“Discreet be the days of your holiness,” said Sancho, “for the good
opinion you have of my wit, though there’s none in me; but the story I
want to tell is this. There was an invitation given by a gentleman of
my town, a very rich one, and one of quality, for he was one of the
Alamos of Medina del Campo, and married to Doña Mencia de Quiñones, the
daughter of Don Alonso de Marañon, Knight of the Order of Santiago,
that was drowned at the Herradura—him there was that quarrel about
years ago in our village, that my master Don Quixote was mixed up in,
to the best of my belief, that Tomasillo the scapegrace, the son of
Balbastro the smith, was wounded in.—Isn’t all this true, master mine?
As you live, say so, that these gentlefolk may not take me for some
lying chatterer.”

“So far,” said the ecclesiastic, “I take you to be more a chatterer
than a liar; but I don’t know what I shall take you for by-and-by.”

“Thou citest so many witnesses and proofs, Sancho,” said Don Quixote,
“that I have no choice but to say thou must be telling the truth; go
on, and cut the story short, for thou art taking the way not to make an
end for two days to come.”

“He is not to cut it short,” said the duchess; “on the contrary, for my
gratification, he is to tell it as he knows it, though he should not
finish it these six days; and if he took so many they would be to me
the pleasantest I ever spent.”

“Well then, sirs, I say,” continued Sancho, “that this same gentleman,
whom I know as well as I do my own hands, for it’s not a bowshot from
my house to his, invited a poor but respectable labourer—”

“Get on, brother,” said the churchman; “at the rate you are going you
will not stop with your story short of the next world.”

“I’ll stop less than half-way, please God,” said Sancho; “and so I say
this labourer, coming to the house of the gentleman I spoke of that
invited him—rest his soul, he is now dead; and more by token he died
the death of an angel, so they say; for I was not there, for just at
that time I had gone to reap at Tembleque—”

“As you live, my son,” said the churchman, “make haste back from
Tembleque, and finish your story without burying the gentleman, unless
you want to make more funerals.”

“Well then, it so happened,” said Sancho, “that as the pair of them
were going to sit down to table—and I think I can see them now plainer
than ever—”

Great was the enjoyment the duke and duchess derived from the
irritation the worthy churchman showed at the long-winded, halting way
Sancho had of telling his story, while Don Quixote was chafing with
rage and vexation.

“So, as I was saying,” continued Sancho, “as the pair of them were
going to sit down to table, as I said, the labourer insisted upon the
gentleman’s taking the head of the table, and the gentleman insisted
upon the labourer’s taking it, as his orders should be obeyed in his
house; but the labourer, who plumed himself on his politeness and good
breeding, would not on any account, until the gentleman, out of
patience, putting his hands on his shoulders, compelled him by force to
sit down, saying, ‘Sit down, you stupid lout, for wherever I sit will
be the head to you; and that’s the story, and, troth, I think it
hasn’t been brought in amiss here.’”

Don Quixote turned all colours, which, on his sunburnt face, mottled it
till it looked like jasper. The duke and duchess suppressed their
laughter so as not altogether to mortify Don Quixote, for they saw
through Sancho’s impertinence; and to change the conversation, and keep
Sancho from uttering more absurdities, the duchess asked Don Quixote
what news he had of the lady Dulcinea, and if he had sent her any
presents of giants or miscreants lately, for he could not but have
vanquished a good many.
